slides.title: Title
notes: Welcome. Premise in one line: three Jamf Pro instances, 1,500+ resources, moved from click-ops to Terraform - and what it took to do that inside a bank.
Quick intros from the slide - name, role, and which part of the story each person tells.

slides.title: Context, requirements, constraints
notes: This is a bank - the constraints are the story. No CLI outside dev means no local applies and no local state: everything flows through VCS-triggered runs.
Staging was meant to mirror production but had drifted - that drift drives both the prod-first decision and the staging rebuild later.

slides.title: Who touches Jamf Pro
notes: Three teams manage resources, one config surface. Support acts on Jamf Pro day to day but doesn't hold resource-management access. Splitting the repo by team would fragment ownership of shared dependencies like categories and scripts.
Auditors don't manage resources, but they do touch Jamf Pro - and because Terraform HCL is self-documenting, the repo can be given straight to them instead of building a separate audit trail.

slides.title: What a Terraform workspace is
notes: Define it plainly first - one set of Terraform code linked to one state file. Walk the diagram left to right: code goes in, the workspace is the boundary that holds the state, the variables and secrets, the permissions and the workflow, and a run comes out as a plan, then a policy check, then an apply against one Jamf Pro instance.

Then make the real point. How you carve an instance into workspaces is worth spending serious time on. Do not rush it. Re-cutting it later means moving state, which is a much harder day than getting the boundaries roughly right at the start.

Take the four lenses in order and give an example of each from our own split rather than reading them out. The last line is the honest caveat - there are more considerations than fit on a slide, and they refine the choice rather than drive it.

slides.title: Migration outcomes we considered and rejected
notes: Expect pushback on "not everything in Terraform" - defend it: troubleshooting must not require a pull request.

slides.title: Migration path options
notes: Three paths were genuinely on the table. Walk each diagram left to right - the left box is where a change lands first, the right box is where it goes next.

On path one the colour is the resource type - scripts, then dock items, then categories - and the same colour appears in both environments, so you can see all of one kind crossing before the next one starts.

Paths one and two both keep staging in the loop while production is still being built, and that is what killed them: staging was not representative, so validating against it proved nothing. Path three leaves staging until production is finished, which is the whole difference between it and path two.

Prod first is counterintuitive on purpose. Importing is read-then-manage - with a read-only API client there is no write surface, so it is safer than it sounds. Write scopes were only widened once imports were stable at zero diff.

slides.title: Prerequisites
notes: The tidy-up mattered - importing dead config would have codified years of cruft. PRUNE found the unused resources; jamf-resource-deleter removed them safely, with a JSON backup and restore path in case anything was needed back. Migration prep sits alongside it: runner line of sight, a backout plan and a check for org-wide policies, agreed before the first import.

slides.title: Singletons first
notes: November 2025 - the first real state in the repo.

Mechanic: import first if the provider supports it - only fall back to apply where there's no import statement. The apply just sets the same values the UI shows, so nothing changes, but the resource lands in state. All settings panes done in about a day.

slides.title: Guardrails you don't own
notes: Why the ban exists: Terraform runs the bank's whole public cloud - import blocks would let one workspace adopt someone else's resources. The policy is right; it just did not fit a sole-actor migration.
Each import window needed a fresh time-bound exception until the standing exception was granted.

slides.title: Resource sequencing
notes: The matrix is a spreadsheet the team built together. Risk scales with dependency fan-in: singletons carry none, scripts and categories and departments stand alone, smart groups and advanced searches and extension attributes sit on top of those, and profiles and policies sit on top of everything - so they close the migration.
Also considered migrating instance-by-instance - rejected in favour of one resource type at a time, end to end.

slides.title: Migration wave workflow
notes: Step 3 is the one people skip and regret - revoking write permissions makes the freeze real rather than polite.
Bulk waves ran December into January.

slides.title: Tools and helpers
notes: jamfpy is Joseph's open-source SDK. Each candidate got a script emitting a structured map, duplicates and all.
generate-config-out rejected: one block per resource; we wanted one block per type, driven by data.
AI use in one line: Copilot CLI validating configuration and dependency links.

slides.title: Dynamic creation with for_each
notes: The technical centrepiece. One block per type; adding category two hundred is a one-line diff; reviews diff data, not boilerplate.
Division of labour: Gordon imported verbosely, Joseph refined in passes - dedup, name the IDs, share the locals - with a zero-diff plan after every pass, through February and March.

slides.title: for_each exceptions
notes: This is the honesty slide - when the map's harder to read than plain HCL, the pattern isn't earning its keep. Policies were the one exception - they're too different from each other for one map to hold, so we kept them in plain HCL.

slides.title: Validating a migration
notes: Gate 4 is the point of no return - and the point of the whole exercise.
State lives in HCP and is not locally inspectable, hence the Copilot CLI checks in gate 2.

slides.title: Rebuilding staging
notes: The highlight - slow down here.

Importing staging would have enshrined years of drift. So: wipe (keep APNS and the cloud IdP), apply production's modules, iterate through the errors until clean. Parity is now inherited, not claimed.

Set up the next two slides: rebuilding staging is what exposed the repo problem. A real staging environment is only useful if you can deploy to it first, and back then a change there mirrored straight to production.

slides.title: Growing pains
notes: The trigger was the staging rebuild: we wanted staging-first deploys without mirroring to production, and the only lever the repo had was an FQDN conditional. They were everywhere before long - deployment behaviour inferred from a URL.
The pivot: modules own configuration, thin per-instance roots own only genuine differences.

slides.title: The module structure
notes: Three workspaces per instance is the blast radius control - guidance says ~500 resources per workspace and the estate holds 1,500+.
Payloads live in the modules too. Staging-only profiles sit in a visible directory, so divergence is explicit.

slides.title: The estate today
notes: Walk the four tiers by role, not by name. Sandbox: isolated, no restrictions, CLI and GUI both open - break it, reset, start again; onboarding and leadership demos live here. DevTest: under IdP and device compliance but not change controlled - prove a change out fast. Staging: an exact replica, to the point that a device enrolled there is indistinguishable bar the MDM certificate - and it is only true because of the rebuild on the previous slide. Production: minimal downtime, because everything upstream has already done the work.
Then CalVer: we defaulted to SemVer like typical devs, but v1.64.3 tells you nothing about a Jamf Pro estate. A date does - roll back to the day the incidents were raised.

slides.title: By the numbers
notes: Split the timeline or the room hears thirteen months of migration. April 2025 is the provider-development start; nothing was imported before November 2025. May 2026 is both v1.0.0 and the final handover, with the Mac engineering team working proficiently on their own.

Close on the handover, not the stats: approaching a thousand pull requests now, and none of the three of us are on that team any more. The estate is still moving. That is the real number on the slide.
